title: Does Job Fear God for Nothing?
summary: Job, a wealthy and blameless man of Uz, lives in reverence toward God and offers sacrifices for his children. In the heavenly court the LORD points to Job's integrity, and the accuser answers that Job serves God only because God has protected and blessed him. Given permission to strike all Job has, the accuser brings disaster in a single day, and Job loses his livestock, servants, and all ten children, yet he worships and does not sin or charge God with wrong.
story: Job opens outside Israel's story. There is no mention of Abraham, Moses, the covenant, or the land. We meet a man from Uz, somewhere east of Israel, whose faith and whose suffering belong to every human being. The prologue alternates between earth and heaven, and the reader is let into a scene Job himself never witnesses. That gap between what the reader knows and what Job knows drives the entire book. Chapter 2 will bring a second test, and then the long poem of chapters 3 to 42 will explore how Job, his friends, and finally God himself respond to suffering that no one on earth can explain.
historical:
The book doesn't say when Job lived, and the date of its writing is debated (see the introduction). The setting feels ancient and patriarchal. Job's wealth is counted in flocks and herds, he acts as priest for his own household, and there is no temple or law of Moses. His 7,000 sheep, 3,000 camels, 500 yoke of oxen, and 500 female donkeys make him, as the text says, the greatest man of all the people of the East, a phrase used for peoples living east of Israel in the desert fringe (compare Judges 6:3).

The raiders fit that world. The Sabeans were probably Arabian people connected with Sheba, whose caravans and raiding parties ranged widely. The Chaldeans here are best understood as tribal raiders from the region of southern Mesopotamia, before the Chaldean dynasty that later ruled Babylon. The location of Uz is uncertain; Lamentations 4:21 links it with Edom, and some scholars place it further north toward Aram.
cultural:
Job's practice of offering burnt offerings for his children after their feasts reflects an old custom in which the head of a family acted as priest, as Noah, Abraham, and Jacob did. A burnt offering was an animal wholly burned on the altar, given entirely to God, and it was offered for atonement and devotion. Job fears that his children may have cursed God in their hearts, and he acts to cover even hidden sin.

The heavenly scene draws on the ancient picture of God as a king surrounded by a council. The sons of God are heavenly beings who serve him and present themselves before him. Among them comes the satan, a Hebrew word meaning adversary or accuser, which here has the definite article, the accuser. Readers disagree about whether this figure is the devil of later Scripture or a member of the court whose role is to test and accuse; see the hard question below. Job's response to loss follows the rites of mourning: he tears his robe, shaves his head, and falls to the ground, signs of grief that were familiar throughout the ancient Near East.
literary: The prologue is written in simple, patterned prose, like a folk story, in contrast with the dense poetry to come. Scenes alternate between earth (verses 1-5), heaven (6-12), and earth again (13-22). Repetition carries the drama. Four messengers arrive one after another, each introduced with the words while he was still speaking and each ending with the same refrain, I alone have escaped to tell you. The disasters alternate between human raiders and natural forces (Sabeans, fire of God, Chaldeans, a great wind), sweeping every part of Job's life. The key question of the book is spoken by the accuser in verse 9, and the key answer is Job's worship in verse 21. The narrator's verdict in verse 22 frames everything that follows.

outline.t: The first scene in the heavenly court

doctrines.note: The accuser can act only with the LORD's permission and within the limit the LORD sets. The chapter insists that nothing, even evil, lies outside God's rule, while leaving the reasons for his permission hidden from Job.

Job suffers not because he is wicked but because he is righteous. The book begins by denying the simple assumption that suffering always follows sin, and every later argument must be measured against this opening.
The accuser claims that Job's faith is a transaction. Job's worship in loss shows that faith can hold on to God for God's own sake, blessing the name of the LORD who both gave and took away.

words.note: Satan, adversary or accuser. In Job the word has the definite article, the satan, which suggests a title or role rather than a personal name. Elsewhere it is used of human adversaries (1 Samuel 29:4) and of the angel who opposes Balaam (Numbers 22:22). Later Scripture uses the word as the name of the devil.

Chinnam, for nothing, without cause, freely. The accuser's question in verse 9 turns on this word: does Job fear God for nothing, with no reward? The same word returns in 2:3, where the LORD says the accuser incited him against Job without cause. The book's central question is built on it.

Barakh, to bless. In verses 5 and 11 (and 2:5, 9) the Hebrew literally says bless, but it is a euphemism for curse, avoiding putting the words curse God directly in writing. Job's own words in verse 21 use the verb in its true sense: blessed be the name of the LORD. The book plays on both meanings.

Tam, blameless, complete, whole. It describes a person of integrity whose life is undivided. It does not mean sinless, but it means that Job's character is sound through and through. The narrator and the LORD both use it, so the reader knows Job's suffering is not punishment.

christ: Job is an innocent sufferer who loses everything and still blesses God, and the New Testament holds him up as an example of perseverance: “You have heard of Job’s perseverance and have seen the outcome from the Lord. The Lord is full of compassion and mercy” (James 5:11). The book does not predict Jesus, but its questions lead toward him. Jesus is the truly innocent one whose loyalty to his Father was tested to the uttermost, who served God not for reward but out of love. Whatever the precise identity of the accuser in Job (see the hard question below), the New Testament takes up the same role of accuser before God and announces its end: Revelation describes “the accuser of our brothers” who “has been thrown down” (Revelation 12:10). Christians have long read the heavenly court of Job 1 as part of the conflict that the cross resolves, a thematic link rather than a prediction.

hard.q: Why would God allow Satan to destroy Job's family as a test, and is this satan the devil?
hard.a: This is one of the hardest scenes in Scripture. Several things are worth noticing. First, the text presents the prologue in the style of a story, and readers differ on how literally to take the heavenly dialogue; some see it as a real glimpse into God's council, others as a dramatic device that sets up the book's question. Second, the accuser, not God, proposes the test and carries out the destruction, but the LORD permits it and sets its limits, and the book never lets God off the hook: Job's own confession says the LORD has taken away, and the narrator says he did not sin in saying so. Third, the book does not claim that this scene explains every human loss; it explains Job's, and it teaches the reader that there may be reasons hidden from sufferers. On the identity of the satan, some scholars argue this is a member of the heavenly court with the role of prosecutor, not yet the fully developed figure of the devil. Others, following the New Testament's picture of the accuser, identify him with Satan, the enemy of God. Either way, he is under God's authority and acts with hostile intent toward Job.

questions: The accuser asks whether Job fears God for nothing. Would your faith survive if the blessings you associate with it were taken away?
Job worships in the moment of his worst loss. What does his response show about grief and faith existing together?
The reader knows what Job doesn't. How does it change your view of suffering to realize that there may be reasons you can't see?
